title: How to Set AI Agent Permissions Without Engineers
summary: AI agent permissions vary significantly across platforms. This comparison helps you choose the right one and decide how much access to safely grant agents.
body_markdown:
## Agent access by platform


On every platform, an agent gets exactly the access you connect, but the controls around that access differ, and the gap is widest at stopping an agent.


In the[BriefScript study](https://thebriefscript.com/ai-agent-governance-controls-study/) , **11 of 12 platform families offer audit logs** , so you can almost always see what an agent did afterward.


Nine of 12 offer approvals, so a human gate before an irreversible step is likely but not guaranteed. **Only 6 of 12 offer revocation** , which means that on half the field, cutting off a misbehaving agent may mean deleting its credentials by hand.


### Zapier and Make


Both are hosted, no-code tools where an agent's reach is the set of app connections you authorize. That suits a team without engineers, because least privilege comes down to which accounts you connect and with what scope.


In exchange, your data runs on the vendor's infrastructure. Check each vendor's current plan page for which tier includes logs and approval steps before you commit.


### n8n and Power Automate


If you self-host n8n, credentials and data stay on your own servers. The cost is that someone on your side must run and patch it, so it fits teams with at least one technical owner.


For organizations already inside Microsoft's tenant, Power Automate fits, because the agent inherits existing identity and permission rules. Outside that tenant, the advantage mostly disappears.


There is no built-in permission model in LangChain and CrewAI, because they are libraries, not products. The agent gets whatever your code gives it, and approvals, logs, and revocation are things you write.


That's maximum flexibility and the weakest default for a team without engineers.


### Activepieces


Activepieces builds agents without code, with an MIT-licensed core and 750 integrations behind it, which means teams without engineers can build and modify workflows themselves.


Its homepage shows what a governed agent looks like: a seven-step flow from a HubSpot lead trigger through an AI agent step, a condition, Salesforce, Slack, a loop, and Gmail, with Human Approval listed as a native capability beside custom logic.


MIT-licensed means the core is open source that anyone may use and self-host, so you can read how its permission controls work instead of taking the vendor's word for it.


An SDK hands an agent code to run, and no tenant, role or audit log comes with it; those belong to a platform, which is why the libraries above leave all three to you.


An agent is a user more than it is code, and Activepieces treats it as one: **RBAC, SSO and SCIM apply to the agent** just as they do to your staff, so they decide which connections it may use as well as what a person may open.


SSO and standard roles come with the Team plan at $200 a month, SCIM and custom RBAC with Ultimate, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production, meaning you're adopting a platform that's proven in demanding, real-world operations.


Open the run detail view for any agent step and each tool call is listed separately with its own input and output, and the enterprise RBAC documentation is where the connection policy is spelled out.


RBAC, short for role-based access control, bundles what a user may use into roles, so an agent can hold a role containing one job's connections and nothing else; custom RBAC lets you write a role of your own when the standard ones are too broad.


SSO means signing in through your company identity provider, so the agent sits behind the same login as your staff. SCIM creates and removes accounts automatically from that provider, so **one change there cuts off an agent** .


Together they give the narrow-credential and revocation controls described earlier somewhere to live, which matters because revocation is the control fewest platforms offer.


The next section builds the agent step by step, where those controls can be checked in practice.
